\chapter{The People You'd Introduce}
\label{ch:sa-people-nouns}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, a family, a brother and a sister in Sanskrit, and say which of those words travelled with English and which quietly did not.}

Say \sk{भगिनी}, name the share-word \sk{भग} it is built on, name \sk{स्वसृ} as the real but non-living PIE cousin of English sister, and run the chapter's four people back together with the roads each one travelled.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mitram]{\sk{मित्रम्} (mitram) — \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} and the god of the given word}

\label{lesson:SA-C11-mitram}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}food,\textquotedblright{} and its gender. (\emph{Annam}; \textbf{neuter}.) The last three words named things you would ask for. This one names someone you would introduce.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मित्रम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{मित्रम्} & \emph{mitram} & \textbf{friend} \\
\sk{मित्रम्} \sk{मम} & \emph{mitram mama} & \textbf{my friend} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{मि}} is \emph{mi}, a short vowel sign under \textbf{\sk{म}}. \textbf{\sk{त्र}} stacks \textbf{\sk{त}} \emph{ta} under \textbf{\sk{र}} \emph{ra}, said as one push, \emph{tra}. \textbf{\sk{म्}} closes it, neuter again: \emph{mi-tra-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{मित्रम्}} comes from Proto-Indo-Iranian \textbf{*mitras}, \textquotedblleft{}that which causes binding\textquotedblright{} — a promise, a pact, a bond between two people. The same word names \textbf{Mithra}, the Avestan and Zoroastrian god of covenant and contract: a friendship, at the root, is a kind of oath.

It travelled east with almost no change at all: Hindi and Marathi \textbf{\sk{मित्र}}, Gujarati \emph{mitra}, all \sk{तत्सम}, lifted straight out of Sanskrit rather than worn down the way \textbf{\sk{पानीयम्}} became \emph{pānī}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a person, grammatically neuter}]
Here is the proof that gender is not about meaning. \textbf{\sk{मित्रम्}} names a person, and Sanskrit still marks it \textbf{neuter} — the same \textbf{-\sk{म्}} you have now seen on water, milk, and food. A noun's gender is a fact about the \emph{word}, inherited with its shape, not a fact about who or what it points to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mitram\textquotedblright{} — friend
  \item the god it shares a name with — \emph{Mithra}
  \item three languages that kept it whole — Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the root behind \sk{मित्रम्} mean, and what god shares it? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}To bind\textquotedblright{}}; \textbf{Mithra}, the covenant god.) Is \sk{मित्र} in Hindi \sk{तत्सम} or \sk{तद्भव}? (\textbf{\sk{तत्सम}}.) What gender is \emph{mitram}, and why is that surprising? (\textbf{Neuter} — it names a person, but gender tracks the word's class, not the person.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṭumbam]{\sk{कुटुम्बम्} (kuṭumbam) — \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} a word that made a round trip}

\label{lesson:SA-C11-kutumbam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} and its gender. (\emph{Mitram}; \textbf{neuter}.) One person's name, now the group everyone belongs to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कुटुम्बम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{कुटुम्बम्} & \emph{kuṭumbam} & \textbf{family}, household \\
\sk{मम} \sk{कुटुम्बम्} & \emph{mama kuṭumbam} & \textbf{my family} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{कु}} is \emph{ku}, a short-\emph{u} sign under \textbf{\sk{क}}. \textbf{\sk{टु}} repeats it under the curled-back \textbf{\sk{ट}}, the retroflex \emph{t} you first met in \textbf{\sk{संस्कृत}}'s neighbours. \textbf{\sk{म्ब}} stacks \textbf{\sk{ब}} \emph{ba} under a silent \textbf{\sk{म्}}, and a final \textbf{\sk{म्}} closes it: \emph{ku-ṭu-mba-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Every etymology so far in this chapter has run from Sanskrit outward. This one runs the other way first. \textbf{\sk{कुटुम्बम्}} is a loanword \textbf{into} Sanskrit from a Dravidian language, compared to Tamil \textbf{kuṭimai}, \textquotedblleft{}family, lineage, allegiance,\textquotedblright{} itself built on \textbf{kuṭi}, \textquotedblleft{}a hut, a settlement.\textquotedblright{} A family, on this account, is literally \emph{those who share one roof}.

From Sanskrit the finished word travelled onward as a formal, learned \sk{तत्सम} — Hindi \textbf{\sk{कुटुंब}} and Bengali \emph{kuṭumbo} — and then made a full circle: Kannada, Telugu and Tamil today all hold this same Sanskrit-shaped form, borrowed back into languages that, on one account, lent Sanskrit the word in the first place.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumbam\textquotedblright{} — family
  \item which family lent Sanskrit the word — Dravidian
  \item the languages that later borrowed it back — Kannada, Telugu, Tamil
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which direction did \sk{कुटुम्बम्} travel first — into Sanskrit, or out of it? (\textbf{Into it} — a Dravidian loanword.) What Tamil word is it compared to, and what does it literally build on? (\textbf{kuṭimai}, \textquotedblleft{}family, lineage,\textquotedblright{} on \textbf{kuṭi}, \textquotedblleft{}a hut.\textquotedblright{}) Which languages later borrowed the Sanskrit-shaped form back? (\textbf{Kannada, Telugu, Tamil}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhrātā]{\sk{भ्राता} (bhrātā) — \textquotedblleft{}brother,\textquotedblright{} the same word, worn two ways}

\label{lesson:SA-C11-bhrata}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}friend.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Kuṭumbam}, \emph{mitram}.) Now for the first person inside that family — and the plainest cousin in this book yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{भ्राता}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{भ्राता} & \emph{bhrātā} & \textbf{brother} \\
\sk{मम} \sk{भ्राता} & \emph{mama bhrātā} & \textbf{my brother} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Masculine — the first noun this chapter has not ended in \textbf{-\sk{म्}}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{भ्रा}} stacks \textbf{\sk{र}} \emph{ra} under \textbf{\sk{भ}} \emph{bha}, one push, then the long-\emph{ā}: \emph{bhrā}. \textbf{\sk{ता}} closes it, \emph{ta} plus long-\emph{ā} again: \emph{bhrā-tā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{भ्राता}} is PIE \textbf{bhrāter-}, and the descent is about as unbroken as this family gets: English \textbf{brother}, Latin \textbf{frāter}, Greek \textbf{phrātēr} are not relatives of \sk{भ्राता} — they \textbf{are} \sk{भ्राता}, six thousand years and three different roads later.

One of those roads runs straight through the daughter languages. \sk{भ्राता} wore down through Prakrit \emph{bhāi} into Bengali \emph{bhāi} and Gujarati \emph{bhāī}, both \sk{तद्भव} — the same word again, just worn smooth by everyday speech rather than lifted whole like \textbf{\sk{मित्र}}.

Grammatically, \sk{भ्राता} is a fossil of its own: an old kinship word built on the stem \textbf{\sk{भ्रातृ}} (\emph{bhrātṛ}), whose nominative singular lengthens the final vowel to \textbf{-\sk{आ}} instead of following the plain patterns you have seen so far.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhrātā\textquotedblright{} — brother
  \item its English, Latin, and Greek selves — brother, frāter, phrātēr
  \item its worn-down grandchildren — \emph{bhāi}, \emph{bhāi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{brother} a cousin of \sk{भ्राता}, or the same word? (\textbf{The same word}, unbroken from PIE.) Which two daughter languages wore it down to \emph{bhāi}? (\textbf{Bengali, Gujarati}.) What gender is \sk{भ्राता}, unlike every noun before it this chapter? (\textbf{Masculine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhaginī]{\sk{भगिनी} (bhaginī) — \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} one with a share}

\label{lesson:SA-C11-bhagini}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}brother,\textquotedblright{} and name the English word it is not a cousin of but literally \textbf{is}. (\emph{Bhrātā}; \textbf{brother}.) The matching word does not tell the same story.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{भगिनी}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{भगिनी} & \emph{bhaginī} & \textbf{sister} \\
\sk{मम} \sk{भगिनी} & \emph{mama bhaginī} & \textbf{my sister} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Feminine — marked by the \textbf{-\sk{ई}} you can hear at the end.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{भ}} is \emph{bha}. \textbf{\sk{गि}} is \textbf{\sk{ग}} \emph{ga} under a short-\emph{i} sign. \textbf{\sk{नी}} closes it, \textbf{\sk{न}} under the long-\emph{ī} sign — the same feminine ending you will meet again this book: \emph{bha-gi-nī}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here the pattern breaks. \sk{भगिनी} is built on \textbf{\sk{भग}} (\emph{bhaga}), \textquotedblleft{}a share, good fortune,\textquotedblright{} plus the feminine suffix \textbf{-\sk{इनी}}: literally, \textquotedblleft{}one with a share.\textquotedblright{}

Sanskrit's actual cousin of English \textbf{sister} is a different word, \textbf{\sk{स्वसृ}} (\emph{svasṛ}), from the same PIE root as \emph{bhrātā}'s. It is real, attested in the old texts — but it did not become the everyday word. \sk{भगिनी} did, and \sk{भगिनी} is what wore down eastward: Bengali \emph{bon} and Gujarati \emph{bahen}, both \sk{तद्भव}, both built on \sk{भग}, not \sk{स्वसृ}.

So the honest connection to draw for \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} is not the one nearest to English. Brother and sister do not travel the same road here — one is the same word worn down; the other took a different word entirely and left the matching one behind.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: four people}]
\emph{Mitram}, \emph{kuṭumbam}, \emph{bhrātā}, \emph{bhaginī} — a friend, a family, a brother, a sister. One borrowed into Sanskrit and then borrowed back out; two travelled in lockstep with their English match; one quietly swapped words along the way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhaginī\textquotedblright{} — sister
  \item what it is built on — \emph{bhaga} \textquotedblleft{}a share\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{-inī}
  \item the word it is NOT built on — \emph{svasṛ}, the real cousin of \emph{sister}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{भगिनी} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}One with a share.\textquotedblright{}}) What is the actual PIE cousin of English \emph{sister}, and why is it not the word we learned? (\textbf{\sk{स्वसृ}} — attested, but never the living word.) Which two daughter languages descend from \sk{भगिनी} instead? (\textbf{Bengali, Gujarati}.) Name this chapter's four people. (\emph{Mitram, kuṭumbam, bhrātā, bhaginī}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\sk{आ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S04-letter-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{अ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{आ}}
\textbf{\sk{आ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{ā} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the joined upper-and-lower left body of \sk{अ}
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item an inner vertical stem
  \item a trailing vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{आ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{आम्} / \sk{न}} \emph{ām / na} — yes / no (ām / na)
  \item \textbf{\sk{आनन्दः}} \emph{ānandaḥ} — joy — and "meeting you is a joy
  \item \textbf{\sk{आगच्छति}} \emph{āgacchati} — he, she, or it comes
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{आ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the inner stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the trailing stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{5.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 4.} The pen comes up 4 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the shared \sk{अ} body into more strokes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{आ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{आ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{आम्} / \sk{न}  ·  \sk{आनन्दः}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{आ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{आ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{आ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ā}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra]{\sk{र} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S110-letter-ra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{◌ि} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{र}}
\textbf{\sk{र}} — \emph{ra}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{r}, it is \textbf{ra}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a top-to-bottom stem curling clockwise around the lower loop
  \item a diagonal tail
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{र} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{नमस्कारः}} \emph{namaskāraḥ} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{}) (namaskāraḥ)
  \item \textbf{\sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय}} \emph{punardarśanāya} — until we meet again (lit. \textquotedblleft{}for seeing again\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\sk{करोमि}} \emph{karomi} — I do, I make (\sk{कार्यं} \sk{करोमि}, \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\sk{एक} \sk{द्व} \sk{त्रि} \sk{चतुर्} \sk{पञ्च}} \emph{eka dva tri catur pañca} — one to five
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{र}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the headline junction, descend the stem, and curl left and clockwise around the lower loop to the tail junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that junction and draw the diagonal tail down-right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source joins the loop and diagonal tail.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{र}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{र} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{नमस्कारः}  ·  \sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{र} three times, saying \emph{ra} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{र} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{र}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ra}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
